answer.why: As an insider, 'Confirmed & Substantive' made me laugh straight away because it is the exact phrasing of a real appointment milestone, and it tells me the developers actually know how the service talks. 'Minister Salary' is the obvious hook, but it sounds like every Singapore salary joke that gets recycled online, and I have heard that one a hundred times at work. I would tap the second to see if they got the details right, and I would be quietly pleased if they did.
answer.expect_minister_salary: A cheeky, satirical clicker about the million-dollar pay debate, probably with a lot of money-counting and a smug 'climb the ladder to get rich' loop. I would expect it to be shallow on how the service really works and to get the grades and processes slightly wrong, aimed at outsiders who want to poke fun at ministerial pay.
answer.expect_confirmed_substantive: A drier, more knowing sim about the quiet grind of a civil service career: appraisals, ranking, postings, waiting to be confirmed in a post and then made substantive. I would expect in-jokes and careful wording that only insiders would notice, with office politics and slow-burn consequences rather than big flashy jackpots. It might be a bit obscure to outsiders, but that is part of the charm.

best_moment.what: Accepting the invitation to tea. The game got the quiet, deniable feel of it right: nothing is offered, nothing is promised, and you both know exactly what is happening.

worst_moment.what: The GE. I picked the GRC route and the result was a single line about 48.2% that said it was never about me. My earlier choices barely seemed to count, and the card read as if it had been decided in advance.

skip_year.why: The utilisation-number year was a tiny spreadsheet dilemma with no visible consequence, and I never saw the recovery plan or the director again.

answer.held_back_by: Not my record. The loss came from the electoral swing and the GRC team, which I only half chose. If anything held me back, it was low REP, since I spent a career doing quiet work that nobody outside the building sees.
answer.ending_fair_why: The card says 'retired at 34' after a loss, which is mostly the game's own abrupt rule rather than a consequence. Nobody in the real service is done at 34 after one GE, and a Perm Sec would be redeployed or offered a statutory board. The loss itself is plausible, but it felt arbitrary for a career spent on integrity.
answer.chase_next: The version where I win the seat or stay in the service. I would build REP early, probably by taking the public-facing postings, to see whether the single-seat route and a ministerial appointment are really reachable.
answer.play_again_why: I want to test whether REP is the hidden stat that gates the political track, and the run was short enough to try again on one MRT ride.

tone_breaks.line: Deputy Secretary at 30, Perm Sec at 32
tone_breaks.note: Ranks run far too fast. Nobody becomes Perm Sec at 32. It breaks the feel of the scholarship track, which is about steady, visible, slow progression.

tone_breaks.line: RETIRED AS Permanent Secretary AT AGE 34
tone_breaks.note: 'Retired' is wrong for someone who lost an election at 34. It would be 'left the service' or 'returned to the private sector'. Real people do not retire there.

tone_breaks.line: it was never going to be about you anyway
tone_breaks.note: A little knowing and fatalistic, and it undercuts the player's agency at the one moment it should count.

answer.title_fit_why: The game works best on appointments, confirmation and the slow grind of the service, not on pay. 'Minister Salary' makes it sound like a cheap jab at pay, which the actual play does not deliver.
